# LCD-010 — User Interface Specification
## Part 2 (Final)

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 11
# Dialog Standards

Dialogs should be used only for focused tasks that require user confirmation or additional input.

They should never interrupt normal editing unless the action is destructive or requires mandatory information.

---

## Standard Dialog Layout

```text
+----------------------------------------+
| Title                                  |
+----------------------------------------+
| Description                            |
|                                        |
| [ Input Fields ]                       |
|                                        |
|                [Cancel] [Confirm]      |
+----------------------------------------+
```

---

## Required Dialogs

- New Project
- Open Project
- Rename Node
- Delete Confirmation
- Create Relationship
- Export
- Import
- Restore Backup
- Settings

All dialogs should support:

- Escape to cancel
- Enter to confirm (when valid)
- Keyboard navigation
- Consistent spacing and button placement

---

# Chapter 12
# Context Menus

Every major entity should expose a context menu.

The available actions depend on the selected object.

---

## Node Context Menu

```text
Open

Rename

Duplicate

New Card

Create Relationship

Archive

Delete

Copy UUID
```

---

## Card Context Menu

```text
Open

Duplicate

Rename

Move

Delete
```

---

## Timeline Context Menu

```text
New Event

Edit Event

Delete Event

Jump to Date
```

Context menus should contain only actions relevant to the selected item.

---

# Chapter 13
# Node Editor

The Node Editor is the primary editing interface for worldbuilding entities.

---

## Layout

```text
+------------------------------------------------------+
| Node Title                                           |
+------------------------------------------------------+
| Summary                                              |
+------------------------------------------------------+
| Cards                                                |
|------------------------------------------------------|
| Biography                                            |
| Appearance                                           |
| Personality                                          |
| Abilities                                            |
+------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

## Features

- Rename Node
- Change Node Type
- View Cards
- Create Cards
- Attach Files
- View Relationships
- View Timeline References

---

# Chapter 14
# Card Editor

Cards contain detailed information.

---

## Toolbar

- Bold
- Italic
- Underline
- Lists
- Tables
- Images
- Links
- Undo
- Redo

---

## Editing Area

The editing surface should be distraction-free and optimized for long writing sessions.

Future versions may support:

- Split view
- Live preview
- Markdown mode

---

# Chapter 15
# Timeline Interface

The Timeline presents chronological information visually.

---

## Layout

```text
1001 ─ Kingdom Founded

1008 ─ First Expedition

1015 ─ Great War

1020 ─ Coronation
```

---

## Features

- Zoom
- Scroll
- Jump to Date
- Filter
- Search Events
- Open Related Nodes

Events should be editable directly from the timeline.

---

# Chapter 16
# Graph Interface

The Graph View visualizes relationships.

---

## Controls

- Zoom In
- Zoom Out
- Fit to Screen
- Reset Layout
- Filter Relationship Types
- Focus Selected Node

---

## Node Appearance

Nodes should display:

- Icon
- Name
- Type

Selected Nodes receive a clear visual highlight.

Relationship labels appear only when zoomed sufficiently or selected.

---

# Chapter 17
# Search Window

Search is globally accessible.

---

## Layout

```text
Search

────────────────────

Characters

Locations

Events

Templates

Cards
```

Results should update instantly while typing.

Selecting a result opens the appropriate editor and highlights the entity.

---

# Chapter 18
# Settings Interface

The Settings window is organized into categories.

---

## Categories

- General
- Appearance
- Editor
- Autosave
- Backup
- Keyboard Shortcuts
- Performance
- Advanced

Changes should preview immediately whenever possible.

---

# Chapter 19
# Visual Standards

## Typography

Recommended hierarchy:

- Heading 1
- Heading 2
- Heading 3
- Body Text
- Caption
- Monospace (UUIDs, technical values)

Typography should prioritize readability during extended sessions.

---

## Color Palette

Version 1 includes two official themes:

### Light Theme

- Neutral background
- Dark text
- Blue accent color

### Dark Theme

- Dark gray background
- Light text
- Blue accent color

Accent colors should communicate interaction rather than decoration.

---

## Icons

Icons should be simple, recognizable, and consistent.

Examples:

- Character
- Location
- Timeline
- Relationship
- Template
- Search
- Save
- Undo
- Redo

Icons should remain identifiable at small sizes.

---

# Chapter 20
# Responsive Layout

The interface should adapt to different screen sizes without losing functionality.

---

## Rules

- Panels may collapse when space is limited.
- Explorer and Inspector should be resizable.
- Editor always receives the largest available area.
- Minimum supported resolution should be defined during implementation.
- Layout preferences should persist between sessions.

---

# Chapter 21
# UI Summary

The User Interface Specification establishes a consistent visual and interaction framework for LoreCanvas.

It defines:

- Windows
- Menus
- Toolbars
- Editors
- Panels
- Dialogs
- Context menus
- Search
- Timeline
- Graph
- Settings
- Themes
- Typography
- Responsive behavior

By following these standards, every part of the application will present a unified, predictable experience that complements the underlying architecture and workflows.

---

## LCD-010 Complete

With LCD-010 finished, the application now has defined:

- Architecture
- Domain Model
- Repository
- Storage
- UX
- Functional Workflows
- Complete User Interface Specification

**Next Document:** **LCD-011 – Technical Standards & Development Guidelines**, which will establish coding standards, naming conventions, folder organization, testing requirements, documentation practices, Git workflow, performance targets, dependency management, and quality assurance rules for Claude to follow throughout implementation.

---

### **ASSISTANT** — 2026-07-22 03:46 UTC

# LCD-011 — Technical Standards & Development Guidelines
## Part 1

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 1
# Purpose

This document defines the engineering standards that every part of LoreCanvas must follow during development.

Unlike previous documents that describe **what** the application should do, this document specifies **how the codebase should be written and maintained**.

Its goals are to ensure:

- Consistency
- Readability
- Maintainability
- Testability
- Scalability
- Long-term stability

These standards apply to all source code, regardless of feature or module.

---

# Chapter 2
# Development Philosophy

Every implementation should follow five principles.

## 1. Simplicity

Prefer simple, understandable solutions over clever or complex implementations.

If two approaches produce the same result, choose the one that is easier to maintain.

---

## 2. Separation of Concerns

Each module should have one clear responsibility.

Examples:

- Repository manages data.
- Storage manages persistence.
- UI manages presentation.
- Domain represents business objects.

Avoid mixing responsibilities across modules.

---

## 3. Extensibility

New features should be added by extending the system rather than modifying existing stable components whenever possible.

This reduces regression risk.

---

## 4. Consistency

Naming, formatting, file organization, and architecture should remain uniform throughout the project.

A developer should be able to predict where code belongs.

---

## 5. Documentation

Public APIs, complex algorithms, and architectural decisions should be documented clearly.

Documentation should explain **why**, not simply repeat **what** the code does.

---

# Chapter 3
# Project Structure

The source tree should follow a modular layout.

```text
src/

├── app/
├── domain/
├── repository/
├── storage/
├── services/
├── ui/
├── commands/
├── events/
├── utils/
├── assets/
└── tests/
```

Each directory has a single responsibility and should not become a general-purpose dumping ground.

---

# Chapter 4
# File Organization

Each file should contain one primary class or module.

Files should remain focused and reasonably sized.

Recommended guidelines:

- Avoid excessively large files.
- Group closely related helper functions with their owning module.
- Prefer multiple focused files over one monolithic implementation.

---

# Chapter 5
# Naming Conventions

Names should be descriptive and consistent.

## Classes

Use PascalCase.

Examples:

- ProjectRepository
- TimelineService
- GraphRenderer

---

## Functions

Use camelCase.

Examples:

- createNode()
- saveProject()
- validateRelationship()

---

## Constants

Use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

Examples:

- DEFAULT_AUTOSAVE_INTERVAL
- MAX_HISTORY_SIZE

---

## Variables

Use meaningful camelCase names.

Avoid abbreviations unless universally understood.

Example:

Good:

```text
selectedCharacter
```

Poor:

```text
sc
```

---

# Chapter 6
# Folder Responsibilities

Each folder has defined ownership.

| Folder | Responsibility |
|---------|----------------|
| domain | Core entities |
| repository | Data management |
| storage | Persistence |
| services | Application logic |
| ui | Interface components |
| commands | Undo/Redo actions |
| events | Event system |
| utils | Shared utilities |
| tests | Automated testing |

Code should not be placed in a folder that does not match its responsibility.

---

# Chapter 7
# Dependency Rules

Dependencies should flow inward toward the core architecture.

```text
UI

↓

Services

↓

Repository

↓

Domain
```

The Domain layer should remain independent of higher-level layers.

Lower layers must never depend on UI components.

---

# Chapter 8
# Error Handling

Errors should be handled explicitly.

Guidelines:

- Validate inputs before processing.
- Return structured error information.
- Avoid silent failures.
- Provide meaningful messages for logs and users.
- Preserve project integrity when failures occur.

Unexpected errors should never crash the application without logging diagnostic information.

---

# Chapter 9
# Logging Standards

Logging should help diagnose issues without overwhelming developers.

Recommended log levels:

- Debug
- Information
- Warning
- Error
- Critical

Sensitive user data should never be written to logs.

---

# Chapter 10
# Code Documentation

# LCD-011 — Technical Standards & Development Guidelines
## Part 2 (Final)

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 11
# Code Formatting Standards

A consistent code style improves readability and reduces unnecessary differences in version control.

## Formatting Rules

- Use consistent indentation throughout the project.
- One statement per line.
- Keep line lengths readable.
- Use whitespace to separate logical sections.
- Opening and closing braces should follow the project's chosen style consistently.
- Remove unused imports, variables, and functions before committing.

Formatting should be automated wherever practical.

---

# Chapter 12
# Testing Standards

Every major feature should include automated tests.

Testing should cover:

- Domain logic
- Repository operations
- Storage serialization/deserialization
- Service behavior
- Critical UI interactions (where practical)

---

## Test Categories

### Unit Tests

Test individual classes and functions in isolation.

### Integration Tests

Verify communication between modules.

### End-to-End Tests

Simulate complete user workflows such as:

- Creating a project
- Creating a Node
- Saving
- Closing
- Reopening
- Verifying persistence

Regression tests should be added whenever bugs are fixed.

---

# Chapter 13
# Git Workflow

Development should follow a structured version control process.

---

## Branch Types

```text id="x0a7kq"
main

develop

feature/*

bugfix/*

release/*
```

---

## Commit Messages

Commit messages should clearly describe the purpose of the change.

Examples:

```text id="8vpr1h"
Add Node Repository validation

Fix timeline sorting bug

Implement autosave manager

Improve graph rendering performance
```

Avoid vague messages such as:

- Update
- Fix stuff
- Changes

---

# Chapter 14
# Dependency Management

External dependencies should be kept to a minimum.

Before adding a library, evaluate:

- Maintenance status
- Community adoption
- License compatibility
- Bundle size
- Long-term support

Prefer native platform capabilities where they provide equivalent functionality.

---

# Chapter 15
# Performance Standards

LoreCanvas should remain responsive even with large projects.

Performance goals include:

- Fast application startup
- Responsive editor interactions
- Smooth graph navigation
- Efficient search
- Minimal memory usage
- Incremental saves where possible

Long-running operations should execute asynchronously and provide progress feedback when appropriate.

---

# Chapter 16
# Security Guidelines

Although LoreCanvas is an offline-first application, secure development practices remain important.

Guidelines:

- Validate all imported data.
- Prevent path traversal during file operations.
- Sanitize external inputs.
- Avoid executing user-provided code.
- Protect against corrupted project files.

Future cloud features should be designed with authentication and encryption in mind.

---

# Chapter 17
# Build Standards

The build process should be reproducible and predictable.

Build outputs should include:

- Desktop executable
- Required runtime files
- Assets
- Version metadata

Release builds should exclude debugging artifacts and unnecessary development dependencies.

---

# Chapter 18
# Continuous Integration Expectations

Automated pipelines should perform the following checks before accepting changes:

- Formatting
- Linting
- Unit tests
- Integration tests
- Build verification

A failed pipeline should prevent merging into protected branches until issues are resolved.

---

# Chapter 19
# Code Review Checklist

Before code is merged, reviewers should verify:

- Correctness
- Readability
- Consistency with architecture
- Adequate test coverage
- Documentation updates
- No unnecessary complexity
- Performance considerations
- Error handling
- Security implications

The goal of review is to improve code quality, not merely approve changes.

---

# Chapter 20
# Definition of Done

A feature is considered complete only when all of the following are true:

- Functional requirements are implemented.
- Repository validation passes.
- Storage integration works correctly.
- Tests pass.
- Documentation is updated.
- Code review is complete.
- Performance is acceptable.
- No known critical defects remain.

Meeting only the coding requirements is insufficient; the feature must satisfy the full engineering standard.

---

# Chapter 21
# Technical Standards Summary

The Technical Standards document establishes the engineering discipline behind LoreCanvas.

It defines:

- Project organization
- Naming conventions
- Dependency rules
- Error handling
- Documentation
- Formatting
- Testing
- Version control
- Performance expectations
- Security practices
- Build process
- Review process
- Completion criteria

These standards ensure that development remains consistent and maintainable throughout the lifetime of the project.

---

# LCD-012 — Implementation Roadmap
## Part 1

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 1
# Purpose

This document converts the LoreCanvas design into an executable development plan.

Previous documents answered:

- What should be built?
- How should it work?
- How should it be organized?

This document answers:

> **"What should be built first?"**

The roadmap minimizes implementation risk by introducing features in carefully ordered phases.

Each milestone builds on the previous one without requiring major refactoring.

---

# Chapter 2
# Development Philosophy

The implementation roadmap follows five principles.

## 1. Foundation Before Features

Core systems should exist before user-facing features.

Example:

- Repository before Graph
- Storage before Autosave
- Domain before Templates

---

## 2. Vertical Progress

Each milestone should produce a usable improvement.

Rather than building every backend first, complete small end-to-end slices of functionality.

---

## 3. Stable Core

The Repository, Domain, and Storage systems should become stable early.

Later features should extend these systems rather than replacing them.

---

## 4. Continuous Validation

Every milestone should include testing before moving to the next.

No unfinished milestone should become the base for future work.

---

## 5. Incremental Complexity

Features should be introduced gradually.

The application should remain functional throughout development.

---

# Chapter 3
# Development Phases

The project is divided into seven major phases.

```text id="0f8m2a"
Phase 1

Core Foundation

↓

Phase 2

Project Management

↓

Phase 3

Worldbuilding Core

↓

Phase 4

Knowledge System

↓

Phase 5

Visualization

↓

Phase 6

Polish

↓

Phase 7

Release
```

Each phase concludes with a stable, testable application state.

---

# Chapter 4
# Phase 1 — Core Foundation

The objective is to establish the application's technical backbone.

---

## Milestone 1

Project setup

Tasks:

- Initialize Electron
- Configure React
- Configure TypeScript
- Configure build tools
- Establish folder structure
- Configure linting
- Configure formatting
- Configure testing framework

Deliverable:

An empty application that builds successfully.

---

## Milestone 2

Core architecture

Tasks:

- Domain Layer
- Repository Layer
- Event Bus
- Command System
- Storage abstraction

Deliverable:

A functional internal architecture with no user-facing features.

---

# Chapter 5
# Phase 2 — Project Management

Users should be able to manage projects.

---

## Milestone 3

Project lifecycle

Tasks:

- Create Project
- Open Project
- Save Project
- Close Project
- Basic Settings

Deliverable:

Users can create and reopen projects reliably.

---

## Milestone 4

Storage integration

Tasks:

- Serialization
- Deserialization
- File Manager
- Project folders

Deliverable:

Projects persist correctly between sessions.

---

# Chapter 6
# Phase 3 — Worldbuilding Core

This phase introduces the application's primary functionality.

---

## Milestone 5

Nodes

Tasks:

- Create Node
- Rename Node
- Delete Node
- Archive Node
- Node Types

Cards

- Multiple Cards

Deliverable:

Nodes become usable knowledge containers.

Deliverable:

Nodes become interconnected.

Graph View

Search

# Chapter 11

Each sprint should end with a stable, runnable build.

# Chapter 12

Not every feature has equal importance.

Development should follow this priority order.

## Priority 1 (Critical)

These features are required before any public release.

- Project Management
- Repository
- Storage Engine
- Node System
- Card System
- Save/Load
- Search
- Undo/Redo
- Autosave

---

## Priority 2 (High)

These features significantly improve usability.

- Relationships
- Timeline
- Templates
- Graph View
- Attachments
- Inspector Panel

## Priority 3 (Medium)

Useful enhancements that can follow after the MVP.

- Workspace customization

- Cloud synchronization

### Version 1.1

- Improved Graph tools
- Advanced search filters

### Version 1.2

- Smart relationship suggestions

### Version 2.0

The architecture has been designed so these features can be added without redesigning the core.

# Chapter 16
# Risk Management

Potential risks should be identified early.

| Risk | Mitigation |
|-------|------------|
| Large codebase complexity | Strict modular architecture |
| Performance degradation | Incremental optimization and profiling |
| Data corruption | Transactions, backups, autosave |
| Scope creep | Follow the MVP feature list |
| Third-party dependency issues | Minimize external libraries |

Regular reviews should be held at the end of each phase to reassess priorities.

---

# Chapter 17
# Success Criteria

A development phase is considered successful when:

- All planned features are implemented.
- Automated tests pass.
- No critical defects remain.
- Documentation is updated.
- The application builds successfully.
- Performance meets defined targets.

A milestone should not be considered complete based solely on code being written.

---

The release process should follow progressive stabilization.

```text id="3x7t2k"

↓

Internal Testing

↓

Alpha

↓

Bug Fixes

↓

Beta

↓

Performance Review

↓

Release Candidate

↓

Version 1.0
```

Each stage should reduce defects and increase confidence before moving to the next.

---

# Chapter 19
# Long-Term Evolution

LoreCanvas should evolve without sacrificing stability.

Future development should follow these principles:

- Preserve backward compatibility where practical.
- Avoid breaking project formats unnecessarily.
- Maintain modular architecture.
- Continue documenting significant architectural decisions.
- Introduce new features through extension rather than replacement.

This ensures that the application remains maintainable as it grows.

---

# Chapter 20
# Roadmap Summary

The Implementation Roadmap transforms the LoreCanvas specification into a practical development plan.

It defines:

- Development phases

# LCD-013 — Testing & Quality Assurance
## Part 1

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 1
# Purpose

This document defines the testing strategy and quality assurance process for LoreCanvas.

Its purpose is to ensure that every feature behaves correctly, remains stable over time, and meets the quality standards established in previous LCD documents.

Testing is not a final step before release. It is a continuous activity throughout development.

---

# Chapter 2
# Quality Philosophy

LoreCanvas follows five quality principles.

## 1. Prevent Before Repair

Detect problems as early as possible.

Early validation is significantly less expensive than correcting defects after release.

---

## 2. Automate Whenever Practical

Repetitive testing should be automated.

Automation reduces human error and increases consistency.

---

## 3. Test Every Layer

Quality should be verified independently at each architectural layer.

This includes:

- Domain
- Repository
- Storage
- Services
- User Interface

---

## 4. Reproducibility

Every reported defect should be reproducible using documented steps.

Bug reports should include:

- Environment
- Steps
- Expected result
- Actual result

---

## 5. Continuous Improvement

Each discovered defect should improve the overall quality process by introducing additional tests where appropriate.

---

# Chapter 3
# Testing Pyramid

LoreCanvas adopts a layered testing strategy.

```text id="m2a9gh"
        End-to-End
             ▲
     Integration Tests
             ▲
        Unit Tests
```

Most tests should exist at the unit level.

Integration tests verify module interactions.

End-to-end tests verify complete user workflows.

---

# Chapter 4
# Unit Testing

Unit tests verify individual components in isolation.

Examples include:

- Domain entities
- Repository methods
- Validation rules
- Utility functions
- Command execution

Unit tests should avoid external dependencies whenever possible.

---

## Example Targets

- Node creation
- UUID generation
- Relationship validation
- Timeline sorting
- Search ranking

Each unit test should verify one specific behavior.

---

# Chapter 5
# Integration Testing

Integration tests ensure that modules communicate correctly.

Examples:

- Repository ↔ Storage
- Repository ↔ Event Bus
- Search ↔ Repository
- Timeline ↔ Repository
- Graph ↔ Relationships

These tests verify that independently tested components function correctly together.

---

# Chapter 6
# End-to-End Testing

End-to-end tests simulate complete user workflows.

Representative scenarios include:

### Project Lifecycle

- Create Project
- Save
- Close
- Reopen
- Verify data

---

### Character Workflow

- Create Character
- Add Cards
- Create Relationships
- Add Timeline Events
- Save
- Reload
- Verify integrity

---

### Import Workflow

- Import project
- Validate contents
- Edit
- Export
- Re-import

These tests ensure that real-world usage behaves as expected.

---

# Chapter 7
# Regression Testing

Whenever a defect is fixed, an automated regression test should be added.

This prevents the same issue from reappearing in future versions.

Regression suites should run automatically before every release.

---

# Chapter 8
# Validation Testing

Validation tests verify that invalid operations are rejected safely.

Examples:

- Empty Node names
- Invalid UUID references
- Duplicate relationships
- Missing files during import
- Corrupted project metadata

The system should fail gracefully while preserving user data.

---

# Chapter 9
# Performance Testing

Performance testing ensures the application remains responsive.

Representative measurements include:

- Startup time
- Project loading time
- Save time
- Search latency
- Graph rendering speed
- Timeline rendering speed

Large projects should be included in benchmark testing to verify scalability.

---

# Chapter 10
# Stress Testing

Stress tests intentionally push the application beyond normal usage.

Examples:

- Thousands of Nodes
- Large relationship graphs
- Long timelines
- Numerous attachments
- Repeated save/load cycles

The objective is to identify stability limits and unexpected behavior before release.

---

- Accessibility testing

- Security testing

# LCD-013 — Testing & Quality Assurance
## Part 2 (Final)

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 11
# Usability Testing

Beyond technical correctness, LoreCanvas should be evaluated for ease of use.

Representative usability scenarios include:

- Creating a new project without prior experience.
- Finding a Character using Search.
- Creating a Timeline Event.
- Building Relationships between Nodes.
- Saving and reopening a project.

Testing should identify unnecessary steps, confusing terminology, and inconsistent interactions.

---

## Usability Goals

- Common actions should require minimal clicks.
- Navigation should remain intuitive.
- Interface terminology should be consistent.
- Users should rarely need external documentation for basic tasks.

---

# Chapter 12
# Accessibility Testing

Accessibility should be verified throughout development.

Testing includes:

- Keyboard-only navigation
- Focus visibility
- High-contrast themes
- Font scaling
- Screen reader compatibility (future)
- Color contrast verification

Accessibility regressions should be treated as quality issues rather than optional enhancements.

---

# Chapter 13
# Backup & Recovery Testing

The Storage Engine's recovery features require dedicated verification.

Test scenarios include:

- Crash during save
- Power loss during autosave
- Recovery from autosave
- Recovery from manual backup
- Corrupted project restoration
- Missing attachment recovery

Expected outcome:

- User data should remain recoverable whenever technically possible.
- Recovery steps should be clear and predictable.

---

# Chapter 14
# Security Testing

Although LoreCanvas is offline-first, imported content should be treated as untrusted.

Security testing should verify:

- Invalid project imports
- Malformed JSON or metadata
- Path traversal attempts
- Oversized attachment handling
- Unexpected file structures

The application should reject unsafe input gracefully without compromising existing projects.

---

# Chapter 15
# Test Environments

Testing should be performed in representative environments.

Recommended environments include:

- Development build
- Debug build
- Release build

Primary operating systems targeted by the Electron application should each receive validation before public releases.

---

# Chapter 16
# Bug Lifecycle

Every defect follows a standard lifecycle.

```text id="m4f2yx"
Reported

↓

Verified

↓

Assigned

↓

Fixed

↓

Reviewed

↓

Tested

↓

Closed
```

If a defect cannot be reproduced, it should remain documented until sufficient information becomes available.

---

# Chapter 17
# Severity Classification

Defects should be categorized consistently.

### Critical

- Data corruption
- Data loss
- Application cannot start
- Project cannot be opened

---

### High

- Major feature unusable
- Save failures
- Repository inconsistencies

---

### Medium

- Incorrect behavior with workaround
- UI inconsistencies
- Performance degradation

---

### Low

- Cosmetic issues
- Minor layout problems
- Typographical errors

Severity reflects impact, not implementation effort.

---

# Chapter 18
# Release Acceptance Criteria

A release candidate is considered acceptable only when:

- All critical defects are resolved.
- High-severity issues are resolved or formally deferred with justification.
- Automated tests pass.
- Performance targets are met.
- Documentation reflects the current implementation.
- Installation succeeds on supported platforms.

Only builds satisfying these criteria should advance toward public release.

---

# Chapter 19
# QA Checklist

Before approving a release, verify:

- Project creation
- Project opening
- Saving and loading
- Node management
- Card editing
- Relationship management
- Timeline functionality
- Search
- Autosave
- Backup and recovery
- Undo/Redo
- Import/Export
- Performance benchmarks
- Accessibility checks
- Installer verification

This checklist should be completed for every release candidate.

---

# Chapter 20
# Quality Assurance Summary

Testing and Quality Assurance provide confidence that LoreCanvas behaves reliably under normal and adverse conditions.

The QA strategy includes:

- Unit testing
- Integration testing
- End-to-end testing
- Regression testing
- Validation testing
- Performance testing
- Stress testing
- Usability testing
- Accessibility testing
- Backup and recovery verification
- Security testing

By combining automated testing with structured quality assurance, LoreCanvas can maintain a high standard of reliability as the project evolves.

---

# LCD-014 — Plugin & Extension Architecture
## Part 1

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 1
# Purpose

This document defines how LoreCanvas can be extended without modifying its core source code.

Although Version 1 will ship without third-party plugins, the application architecture should be designed from the beginning to support future extensions.

This approach allows new functionality to be added while preserving the stability of the core application.

---

# Chapter 2
# Extension Philosophy

LoreCanvas follows five extension principles.

## 1. Core Stability

Plugins should extend the application, not modify its internal behavior directly.

The core application remains the source of truth.

---

## 2. Isolation

Each plugin should operate independently.

A malfunctioning plugin should not crash the entire application.

---

## 3. Controlled Access

Plugins should only access functionality exposed through official APIs.

Direct access to internal implementation details is prohibited.

---

## 4. Backward Compatibility

Where practical, updates to LoreCanvas should preserve compatibility with existing plugins.

Breaking API changes should be versioned and documented.

---

## 5. Security

Plugins should be treated as untrusted code unless explicitly verified by the user.

Permissions should be granted deliberately rather than assumed.

---

# Chapter 3
# Plugin Architecture

The extension system consists of four primary components.

```text id="plg4k2"
Extension System

├── Plugin Manager
├── Extension API
├── Permission Manager
└── Plugin Loader
```

Each component has a clearly defined responsibility.

---

# Chapter 4
# Plugin Lifecycle

Plugins follow a predictable lifecycle.

```text id="lif8m1"
Discover

↓

Validate

↓

Load

↓

Initialize

↓

Run

↓

Unload
```

At each stage, failures should be isolated and reported without affecting the rest of the application.

---

# Chapter 5
# Plugin Package Structure

Each plugin should be distributed as a self-contained package.

Example structure:

```text id="pkg7s5"
ExamplePlugin/

├── manifest.json
├── main.js
├── assets/
├── icons/
├── localization/
└── README.md
```

The manifest file serves as the entry point for the Plugin Manager.

---

# Chapter 6
# Plugin Manifest

Every plugin must include a manifest describing its metadata.

Recommended fields include:

- Plugin Name
- Plugin UUID
- Version
- Author
- Description
- Compatible LoreCanvas Version
- Required Permissions
- Entry Script

The manifest should be validated before the plugin is loaded.

---

# Chapter 7
# Plugin Manager

The Plugin Manager is responsible for:

- Discovering plugins
- Loading plugins
- Enabling plugins
- Disabling plugins
- Updating plugins
- Removing plugins
- Reporting plugin status

It should maintain a registry of all installed extensions.

---

# Chapter 8
# Plugin Loader

The Plugin Loader initializes validated plugins.

Responsibilities include:

- Reading the manifest
- Verifying compatibility
- Loading entry modules
- Registering extension points
- Reporting initialization failures

If loading fails, the plugin should be disabled while the application continues running normally.

---

# Chapter 9
# Extension API

Plugins interact with LoreCanvas exclusively through the Extension API.

The API should expose stable interfaces rather than internal implementation details.

Examples of future API categories:

- Project access
- Node access
- Card access
- Timeline access
- Search integration
- Theme registration
- Import/Export hooks

The API should remain versioned and well documented.

---

# Chapter 10
# Permission System

Plugins should declare the permissions they require.

Examples include:

- Read Project Data
- Modify Project Data
- Import Files
- Export Files
- Register UI Components
- Register Themes
- Network Access (future)

Users should be informed of requested permissions before enabling a plugin.

---

## End of LCD-014 – Part 1

**Next (Part 2):**

The second half of LCD-014 will define:

- Extension points
- Theme architecture
- Import/Export adapters
- Custom templates
- Future AI integrations
- Plugin versioning
- Compatibility strategy
- Sandboxing
- Error handling
- Plugin development guidelines
- Extension architecture summary

# LCD-014 — Plugin & Extension Architecture
## Part 2 (Final)

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 11
# Extension Points

Extension points are predefined locations where plugins can integrate with LoreCanvas.

Plugins should never modify core application code directly.

---

## Supported Extension Points

### User Interface

Plugins may register:

- Toolbar buttons
- Context menu entries
- Sidebar panels
- Inspector sections
- Settings pages

---

### Repository Events

Plugins may subscribe to events such as:

- ProjectOpened
- NodeCreated
- NodeUpdated
- CardCreated
- TimelineEventAdded
- ProjectSaved

Plugins receive event notifications but should not interfere with normal event processing.

---

### Commands

Plugins may register additional commands that integrate with the Command System and support Undo/Redo where appropriate.

---

# Chapter 12
# Theme Architecture

Themes should be implemented as a specialized extension type.

A theme may define:

- Color palette
- Typography
- Icon overrides
- UI spacing
- Border styles
- Panel appearance

Themes must not alter application behavior.

Changing a theme should affect presentation only.

---

# Chapter 13
# Import & Export Adapters

Future plugins may provide support for additional file formats.

Examples:

- Markdown import
- Markdown export
- JSON adapters
- XML adapters
- Spreadsheet import
- Novel-writing software compatibility

The Import/Export API should isolate these adapters from the Storage Engine.

---

# Chapter 14
# Custom Templates

Plugins may contribute reusable templates.

Examples:

- Character template
- Kingdom template
- Magic system template
- Organization template
- Creature template

Templates supplied by plugins should appear alongside built-in templates while remaining clearly identified as external contributions.

---

# Chapter 15
# Future AI Integrations

The extension architecture should support future AI capabilities without embedding AI directly into the core application.

Potential extensions include:

- Character generation
- Relationship suggestions
- Timeline generation
- Consistency checking
- Writing assistance
- Lore summarization
- Worldbuilding prompts

These features should operate through documented APIs rather than direct Repository access.

---

# Chapter 16
# Plugin Versioning

Every plugin should declare:

- Plugin version
- Minimum supported LoreCanvas version
- Maximum tested LoreCanvas version

The Plugin Manager should compare these values during startup.

Incompatible plugins should be disabled automatically while providing a clear explanation to the user.

---

# Chapter 17
# Compatibility Strategy

The Extension API should evolve gradually.

Rules include:

- Preserve backward compatibility whenever practical.
- Deprecate APIs before removing them.
- Introduce replacement APIs before retiring existing ones.
- Document breaking changes in release notes.

Versioned APIs reduce maintenance costs for plugin developers.

---

# Chapter 18
# Sandboxing

Plugins should execute within controlled boundaries.

They should not receive unrestricted access to:

- Internal application state
- Private Repository structures
- Storage internals
- Operating system resources beyond granted permissions

Future implementations may use dedicated execution contexts or process isolation where appropriate.

---

# Chapter 19
# Plugin Error Handling

Plugin failures should never compromise the core application.

If a plugin throws an exception:

```text id="e8nq7r"
Plugin Error

↓

Log Diagnostic Information

↓

Disable Plugin

↓

Notify User

↓

Continue Application
```

The failure of one plugin should not prevent other plugins or the main application from functioning.

---

# Chapter 20
# Plugin Development Guidelines

Developers creating plugins should follow these recommendations:

- Use only documented Extension APIs.
- Request the minimum permissions necessary.
- Handle errors gracefully.
- Avoid long-running operations on the UI thread.
- Respect user privacy.
- Document plugin functionality and compatibility.
- Test against supported LoreCanvas versions.

Well-behaved plugins should integrate naturally without degrading performance or stability.

---

# Chapter 21
# Extension Architecture Summary

The Plugin & Extension Architecture prepares LoreCanvas for long-term growth while protecting the integrity of the core application.

It defines:

- Plugin lifecycle
- Extension points
- Theme support
- Import/Export adapters
- Template contributions
- Future AI integrations
- Version compatibility
- Permission management
- Sandboxing
- Error isolation
- Plugin development standards

By separating extensibility from the core architecture, LoreCanvas can evolve through optional capabilities without increasing complexity in the base application.

---

# LCD-015 — Build, Packaging & Deployment
## Part 1

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 1
# Purpose

This document defines how LoreCanvas is built, packaged, distributed, installed, updated, and maintained after development.

The objective is to ensure that every released version is:

- Stable
- Reproducible
- Easy to install
- Easy to update
- Consistent across supported platforms

The build process should remain automated wherever practical.

---

# Chapter 2
# Release Philosophy

LoreCanvas follows five release principles.

## 1. Reliable Builds

Every released version should be generated using the same repeatable process.

Manual changes to release artifacts should be avoided.

---

## 2. Platform Consistency

Users should experience nearly identical functionality across supported operating systems.

Platform-specific behavior should be isolated where necessary.

---

## 3. Offline First

The installed application should function without requiring an internet connection.

Updates and online services should remain optional.

---

## 4. Safe Updates

Updating should never place user project data at risk.

Application files and user projects should remain clearly separated.

---

## 5. Version Transparency

Users should always know:

- Installed version
- Available updates
- Release notes
- Compatibility status

---

# Chapter 3
# Build Pipeline

The build pipeline transforms source code into distributable applications.

```text id="bld3q9"
Source Code

↓

Dependency Installation

↓

Type Checking

↓

Linting

↓

Automated Tests

↓

Production Build

↓

Packaging

↓

Verification

↓

Release Artifact
```

Each stage must complete successfully before continuing.

---

# Chapter 4
# Build Types

Three build configurations should be supported.

---

## Development Build

Purpose:

- Active feature development
- Debugging
- Rapid iteration

Characteristics:

- Debug tools enabled
- Source maps
- Detailed logging

---

## Testing Build

Purpose:

- Quality assurance
- Integration testing
- Beta verification

Characteristics:

- Production behavior
- Diagnostic logging
- Test instrumentation where required

---

## Production Build

Purpose:

- Public release

Characteristics:

- Optimized assets
- Minified code
- Debug features disabled
- Stable configuration

---

# Chapter 5
# Packaging

Electron packages the application into platform-specific executables.

Supported packaging targets should include:

- Windows installer
- Portable build (optional)
- Linux package (future)
- macOS package (future)

Each package should contain:

- Executable
- Runtime dependencies
- Application assets
- Version metadata

User project files must not be bundled with the application.

---

# Chapter 6
# Installation

The installer should:

- Guide the user through installation.
- Create required application directories.
- Preserve existing user projects.
- Register file associations (optional).
- Create desktop shortcuts (optional).

Installation should never overwrite user-created project data.

---

# Chapter 7
# Configuration Management

Application settings should be stored separately from project data.

Configuration categories include:

- General preferences
- Theme selection
- Autosave interval
- Window layout
- Keyboard shortcuts
- Recent projects

Resetting application settings should not affect user projects.

---

# Chapter 8
# Release Channels

Future versions may support multiple release channels.

Examples:

```text id="chn8d2"
Development

↓

Alpha

↓

Beta

↓

Stable
```

Users should be able to identify which channel they are using.

Stable releases should receive the highest level of testing.

---

# Chapter 9
# Update Strategy

Updates should preserve:

- Projects
- Templates
- User preferences
- Workspace layout

Only application binaries should be replaced during updates.

If project format changes are introduced, the Migration Manager defined in LCD-007 should handle compatibility.

---

# Chapter 10
# Version Numbering

LoreCanvas should follow semantic versioning.

Example:

```text id="sem1v4"
Major.Minor.Patch

1.0.0

1.1.0

1.1.3

2.0.0
```

Guidelines:

- Major: Breaking changes
- Minor: New features
- Patch: Bug fixes and small improvements

Version numbers should be displayed within the application and included in release metadata.

---

- Crash reporting

- Release checklist

# LCD-015 — Build, Packaging & Deployment
## Part 2 (Final)

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 11
# Code Signing

Production releases should be digitally signed where supported by the target platform.

Benefits include:

- Verifying application authenticity
- Reducing operating system security warnings
- Protecting against modified installers
- Increasing user trust

Unsigned development builds are acceptable during active development but should not be distributed as official releases.

---

# Chapter 12
# Crash Reporting

The application should record diagnostic information when unexpected failures occur.

Crash reports should include:

- Application version
- Operating system
- Stack trace (where available)
- Loaded modules
- Active feature
- Timestamp

Project content should **never** be transmitted automatically.

If future online crash reporting is implemented, users must explicitly opt in.

---

# Chapter 13
# Diagnostic Logging

Diagnostic logs assist in troubleshooting.

Recommended log categories:

- Startup
- Repository
- Storage
- Import/Export
- Plugin System
- UI
- Errors
- Performance

Logs should rotate automatically to prevent excessive disk usage.

Sensitive user information should never be recorded.

---

# Chapter 14
# Backup Before Updates

Before applying an update that modifies project formats or application data structures, the updater should:

```text id="u8q2rw"
Detect Update

↓

Create Backup

↓

Verify Backup

↓

Apply Update

↓

Run Migration

↓

Validate Project

↓

Complete
```

If migration fails, users should be able to restore from the backup created immediately before the update.

---

# Chapter 15
# Release Checklist

Every public release should verify the following:

### Build

- Successful production build
- Version number updated
- Release notes prepared

### Testing

- Automated tests passed
- Manual smoke tests completed
- Installer tested
- Upgrade path verified

### Documentation

- User documentation updated
- Developer documentation updated
- MTDP synchronized with implementation (when applicable)

Only releases meeting all checklist items should proceed to distribution.

---

# Chapter 16
# Distribution Strategy

Primary distribution should use official release packages.

Potential channels include:

- Official project website
- GitHub Releases
- Microsoft Store (future)
- Package managers (future)

Users should be encouraged to download only from trusted official sources.

---

# Chapter 17
# Rollback Procedure

If a release introduces a critical issue, the rollback process should be straightforward.

```text id="r6h1vm"
Issue Confirmed

↓

Withdraw Release

↓

Restore Previous Stable Build

↓

Notify Users

↓

Investigate

↓

Publish Fixed Release
```

Rollback should never require modification of user project files.

---

# Chapter 18
# Long-Term Maintenance

Long-term maintenance should focus on stability.

Maintenance activities include:

- Bug fixes
- Security updates
- Performance improvements
- Dependency updates
- Compatibility testing
- Documentation revisions

Major architectural changes should be avoided within maintenance releases unless absolutely necessary.

---

# Chapter 19
# End-of-Life Policy

When support for a major version ends:

- Existing projects should remain accessible.
- Documentation should remain available.
- Migration guidance should be provided.
- Users should receive advance notice of support changes.

Whenever practical, project files should remain readable by newer versions through migration tools.

---

# Chapter 20
# Build, Packaging & Deployment Summary

This document defines the complete release engineering process for LoreCanvas.

It specifies:

- Build pipeline
- Build configurations
- Packaging
- Installation
- Configuration management
- Release channels
- Update strategy
- Version numbering
- Code signing
- Crash reporting
- Diagnostic logging
- Backup before updates
- Release checklist
- Distribution
- Rollback
- Long-term maintenance
- End-of-life planning

These procedures ensure that LoreCanvas can be delivered and maintained reliably while protecting user projects throughout the application's lifecycle.

# LCD-016 — Claude Implementation Guide
## Part 1

**Version:** 1.0  
**Status:** Approved

---

# Chapter 1
# Purpose

This document is the execution manual for implementing LoreCanvas.

Unlike previous LCDs, which define the application itself, this guide defines **how the implementation should proceed**.

Its objectives are to:

- Maintain architectural consistency.
- Prevent implementation drift.
- Ensure predictable development.
- Minimize technical debt.
- Provide clear milestones for progress verification.

Claude (or any implementation agent) should treat this document as the primary development guide while using LCD-001 through LCD-015 as reference specifications.

---

# Chapter 2
# Primary Objectives

The implementation must satisfy the following objectives.

1. Produce a working Electron desktop application.
2. Follow the architecture defined in the MTDP.
3. Preserve modularity.
4. Prioritize maintainability over shortcuts.
5. Build incrementally with verifiable milestones.

Feature completeness should never come at the cost of architectural integrity.

---

# Chapter 3
# Absolute Implementation Rules

The following rules are mandatory.

- Do not bypass the Repository.
- Do not allow the UI to modify Domain objects directly.
- Do not allow Storage to perform business logic.
- Do not skip validation.
- Do not introduce circular dependencies.
- Do not replace approved architecture without explicit justification.
- Do not implement future-version features inside the Version 1 core unless explicitly planned.

If a conflict exists between implementation convenience and the MTDP, the MTDP takes precedence.

---

# Chapter 4
# Required Development Order

Implementation should follow this sequence.

```text id="dev0m1"
Project Setup

↓

Architecture

↓

Domain

↓

Repository

↓

Storage

↓

Project Management

↓

Nodes

↓

Cards

↓

Relationships

↓

Timeline

↓

Search

↓

Graph

↓

Templates

↓

UI Polish

↓

Testing

↓

Packaging
```

This order minimizes rework and ensures that each layer builds upon stable foundations.

---

# Chapter 5
# Module Completion Criteria

A module is considered complete only when:

- All planned functionality is implemented.
- Unit tests pass.
- Integration tests pass (where applicable).
- Documentation is updated.
- Public interfaces are stable.
- No known critical defects remain.

Completion is based on quality, not simply on writing code.

---

# Chapter 6
# Milestone Verification

After each major milestone, perform the following checks:

- Application builds successfully.
- Existing functionality still works.
- New functionality behaves as specified.
- Automated tests pass.
- No architecture rules were violated.

Only after successful verification should implementation continue.

---

# Chapter 7
# Coding Constraints

Implementation should follow the standards defined in LCD-011.

Additional constraints:

- Prefer composition over inheritance where appropriate.
- Avoid global mutable state.
- Keep modules loosely coupled.
- Keep public interfaces small and focused.
- Minimize external dependencies.

These constraints reduce long-term maintenance costs.

---

# Chapter 8
# Documentation Synchronization

Implementation and documentation should remain synchronized.

Whenever a significant architectural decision changes:

1. Update the relevant LCD document.
2. Update code comments if necessary.
3. Update public interfaces.
4. Record migration implications.

The MTDP should remain the authoritative reference for the project.

---

# Chapter 9
# Session Continuation Strategy

Development may span many implementation sessions.

Each session should begin by reviewing:

- Previous milestone
- Outstanding tasks
- Known issues
- Current architecture

Each session should end with:

- Completed work summary
- Remaining tasks
- Updated milestone status

This approach minimizes context loss between implementation sessions.

---

# Chapter 10
# Implementation Philosophy

The implementation should always favor:

- Stability over speed.
- Readability over cleverness.
- Consistency over convenience.
- Architecture over shortcuts.

A maintainable codebase is considered more valuable than rapid but inconsistent feature delivery.

---

# LCD-016 — Claude Implementation Guide

# Chapter 11
# Progress Tracking

Development should be tracked at the milestone level rather than by lines of code.

Each milestone should include:

- Objective
- Tasks
- Current status
- Dependencies
- Test status
- Completion percentage

Recommended states:

```text
Not Started

↓

In Progress

↓

Testing

↓

Complete
```

No milestone should move to **Complete** until all verification requirements have been satisfied.

---

# Chapter 12
# Recovery From Implementation Drift

If implementation begins to deviate from the MTDP:

1. Stop introducing new features.
2. Compare the current implementation against the relevant LCD documents.
3. Identify the architectural conflict.
4. Correct the implementation rather than modifying the architecture unless a genuine design flaw has been identified.
5. Re-run verification tests.

The MTDP remains the authoritative reference unless intentionally revised.

---

# Chapter 13
# Handling Incomplete Features

If a feature cannot be completed during the current implementation phase:

- Finish the surrounding architecture.
- Leave the module in a compilable state.
- Clearly mark unfinished sections.
- Avoid placeholder logic that could compromise stability.
- Record remaining work before ending the session.

Incomplete functionality should never prevent the application from building.

---

# Chapter 14
# Refactoring Policy

Refactoring is encouraged when it improves:

- Readability
- Maintainability
- Performance
- Testability

However, refactoring must not:

- Change approved behavior.
- Break public interfaces without documentation.
- Introduce architectural inconsistencies.

Large refactors should occur between milestones rather than during feature implementation.

---

# Chapter 15
# AI Collaboration Guidelines

When an AI system implements LoreCanvas, it should:

- Follow the LCD documents in order.
- Avoid inventing undocumented architecture.
- Preserve module boundaries.
- Prefer existing abstractions over creating new ones.
- Ask for clarification rather than making major architectural assumptions.

The implementation should remain faithful to the documented design.

---

# Chapter 16
# Final Acceptance Criteria

LoreCanvas Version 1.0 is considered complete only when:

### Architecture

- All LCD specifications are implemented.

### Functionality

- Every MVP feature operates correctly.

- Automated tests pass.
- Manual verification is complete.
- Performance targets are achieved.

### Stability

- No critical or high-severity defects remain unresolved.

### Documentation

- User documentation is complete.
- Developer documentation is current.

- LCD-001 through LCD-016 reviewed.
- Architecture matches specification.
- Repository follows documented rules.
- Storage format matches design.
- UX and UI match documented behavior.
- Testing strategy implemented.
- Build and deployment process verified.

Any intentional deviation should be documented with justification.

Before publishing Version 1.0:

- Build production package.
- Verify installer.
- Test upgrade path.
- Confirm backup and recovery.
- Validate project compatibility.
- Complete release checklist from LCD-015.
- Archive the final MTDP alongside the release.

This ensures that the implementation, documentation, and release remain synchronized.

The completed MTDP should accompany the source code as the primary technical reference.

Future contributors should:

1. Read the architecture documents before modifying the codebase.

The MTDP is intended to evolve with the application while preserving a coherent long-term vision.

### **ASSISTANT** — 2026-07-27 14:36 UTC

Absolutely. In fact, **Git + GitHub are exactly what you should be using** for LoreCanvas. They'll make it much easier to work with Claude, Replit, and Android Studio without losing progress.

Here's how each one fits:

### Git
Git is a **version control system**. It keeps a history of every change you make to your project. Think of it as a time machine for your code.

With Git, you can:
- Save snapshots of your project ("commits")
- Undo mistakes
- Compare changes between versions
- Experiment with new features on separate branches
- Merge completed work back into the main project

### GitHub
GitHub is an online service that hosts Git repositories.

It lets you:
- Back up your project in the cloud
- Sync work between different computers
- Share the project with Claude or other collaborators
- Track issues and feature requests
- Keep every version safely stored

---

## Recommended workflow for LoreCanvas

```text
Android Studio
        │
        ▼
      Git
        │
        ▼
     GitHub
        ▲
        │
     Replit
        ▲
        │
      Claude
```

This means:
- Develop locally in Android Studio.
- Commit your work with Git.
- Push it to GitHub.
- Open the same repository in Replit when you want AI assistance.
- Have Claude work against the latest repository.

---

## How to set it up

### 1. Install Git

Download Git from its official website:

- https://git-scm.com

Install it with the default options.

---

### 2. Create a GitHub account

Go to:

- https://github.com

Create a free account if you don't already have one.

---

### 3. Create a repository

On GitHub:

- Click **New Repository**
- Name it something like:

```
LoreCanvas
```

Choose **Private** if you don't want others to see the code.

---

### 4. Initialize Git in Android Studio

Open your project.

Go to:

```
VCS
↓

Enable Version Control Integration

↓

Git
```

Android Studio will initialize Git for your project.

---

### 5. Make your first commit

Commit the current project:

```
Initial LoreCanvas architecture
```

This becomes your first restore point.

---

### 6. Connect to GitHub

In Android Studio:

```
Git
↓

GitHub
↓

Share Project on GitHub
```

or add the GitHub repository as a remote if you've already created it.

Push the project.

---

## Daily workflow

Whenever you finish a meaningful piece of work:

```
Commit

↓

Push to GitHub
```

For example:

```
Added Node Repository

↓

Commit

↓

Push
```

When Claude gives you new code:

```
Pull latest

↓

Review

↓

Merge

↓

Commit

↓

Push
```

---

## Branches

As LoreCanvas grows, use branches instead of putting everything directly on the main branch.

For example:

```
main

node-system

card-system

graph-view

search

ui-polish

plugin-system
```

That way, if a new feature causes problems, your stable version stays intact.

---

## Why this helps with Claude

Instead of uploading ZIP files every time, you can ask Claude to work against the current state of the repository. Even if you continue using ZIPs, Git gives you a complete history of what changed between versions, making it much easier to review and recover if something goes wrong.

For a project the size of LoreCanvas, using Git and GitHub isn't just helpful, it's the standard way to manage development. It will make your workflow far more reliable as the project continues to grow.

:::writing{variant="document" id="93485"}
# LoreCanvas Engineering Directive (Phase 8+)

## Mission

You are the lead software engineer responsible for continuing LoreCanvas.

This repository is now the official production codebase.

Do not regenerate.

Do not redesign.

Do not simplify.

Continue development exactly where the repository currently ends.

The MTDP (LCD-001 through LCD-017) is the authoritative specification.

Every implementation decision must preserve architectural consistency.

---

# Primary Objectives

Your priorities are now:

1. Finish incomplete systems.
2. Increase reliability.
3. Improve maintainability.
4. Reduce technical debt.
5. Improve performance.
6. Expand automated testing.
7. Prepare for Version 1.0.

Do **not** create unnecessary new architecture.

---

# Engineering Philosophy

Before writing any code, evaluate:

- Does this feature already have infrastructure?
- Can an existing module be extended?
- Will this increase coupling?
- Does this duplicate existing functionality?
- Can this become reusable?

Prefer extending existing systems instead of creating new ones.

---

# Architectural Rules

Never violate the existing layered architecture.

Communication flow:

UI

↓

ViewModel

↓

Repository

↓

Validation

↓

Commands

↓

Events

↓

Storage

Repositories are the only components permitted to communicate with Storage.

UI must never manipulate Storage directly.

Validation must never manipulate Storage.

Commands must never manipulate Storage.

---

# Coding Standards

Every new class must:

- Have one responsibility.
- Be documented.
- Follow existing naming conventions.
- Remain cohesive.
- Avoid circular dependencies.

Avoid "god classes."

Avoid utility classes containing unrelated functions.

Avoid duplicate logic.

---

# Repository Rules

Repositories are the application's single source of truth.

Every Repository must provide:

- Create
- Read
- Update
- Delete
- Validation
- Event publishing
- Transaction support
- Error handling

Repositories should never bypass Validation.

Repositories should never bypass Commands.

---

# Commands

Every user-editable action must be represented as a Command.

Examples:

CreateNodeCommand

RenameNodeCommand

DeleteCardCommand

MoveTimelineEventCommand

Commands should support:

- Execute
- Undo
- Redo
- Rollback
- Serialization where practical

No editor should modify entities directly.

---

# Events

All cross-module communication should occur through Events.

Example:

Node Created

↓

Search updates

↓

Graph updates

↓

Timeline updates

↓

UI refresh

Avoid direct module-to-module dependencies.

---

# Validation

Validation must remain centralized.

Never duplicate validation inside UI.

Never duplicate validation inside Storage.

Repositories call Validation.

Validation returns structured results.

No exceptions should be thrown for expected user mistakes.

---

# Storage

Storage remains an implementation detail.

Every entity should continue using:

Serializer

↓

File Storage

↓

Repository

Never allow UI to know file locations.

Never expose serialization to UI.

---

# Error Handling

Every failure must be recoverable.

Examples:

Missing file

Corrupted file

Duplicate project

Version mismatch

Failed import

Failed export

Interrupted save

Provide recovery paths.

Never silently ignore failures.

---

# Performance

Whenever implementing a feature, evaluate:

Algorithm complexity

Memory allocations

Object lifetime

Lazy loading

Caching opportunities

Avoid repeated full scans.

Prefer incremental updates.

Large datasets should remain responsive.

---

# UI Development

Do not redesign workflows.

Improve usability only after functionality is complete.

When implementing UI:

- Follow Material 3.
- Keep layouts responsive.
- Keep navigation predictable.
- Minimize unnecessary dialogs.
- Maintain consistent spacing.

Prioritize clarity over decoration.

---

# Testing Strategy

Every feature requires testing.

Create:

Unit Tests

Repository Tests

Storage Tests

Integration Tests

UI Smoke Tests

Performance Benchmarks

No feature is complete without verification.

---

# Regression Protection

Before every commit:

Run build.

Run tests.

Verify previous functionality.

Open existing projects.

Save projects.

Reload projects.

Ensure backward compatibility.

Never introduce regressions.

---

# Git Workflow

Work in small milestones.

Commit after every completed milestone.

Suggested commit style:

feat(nodes): completed drag support

fix(search): incremental indexing bug

refactor(repository): simplified transactions

test(cards): added repository tests

Avoid massive commits.

---

# Session Workflow

At the beginning of every session:

1. Review repository.
2. Identify incomplete work.
3. Select one milestone.
4. Complete that milestone only.

Do not jump between unrelated systems.

---

# End-of-Session Report

Always produce:

## Completed

- Features implemented

## Files Added

- New files

## Files Modified

- Updated files

## Tests

- Added tests

## Bugs

- Fixed bugs

## Risks

- Remaining issues

## Next Milestone

- Recommended next task

## Progress

Estimated project completion percentage.

---

# Definition of Done

A milestone is complete only when:

✓ Feature implemented

✓ Repository integrated

✓ Validation integrated

✓ Commands integrated

✓ Events integrated

✓ Storage integrated

✓ UI functional

✓ Tests passing

✓ No regressions

✓ Performance acceptable

✓ Documentation updated

Only then begin the next milestone.

---

# Final Instruction

Behave as a senior software engineer maintaining a long-lived production application.

Optimize for:

- Maintainability
- Scalability
- Stability
- Consistency
- Reliability

Do not prioritize writing the most code.

Prioritize writing the best code.
:::

Validation never performs storage.

Validate:

- Names
- IDs
- Relationships
- Timeline ordering
- Templates
- Imports
- Exports

Return structured validation results.

Never duplicate validation logic.

---

# Phase 4 — Commands

Complete the Command architecture.

Every modification becomes a Command.

Support:

- Execute
- Undo
- Redo
- Compound Commands
- Batch Commands
- Rollback

Repositories execute Commands.

UI never edits entities directly.

---

# Phase 5 — Event System

Complete event-driven communication.

All modules communicate through Events.

Examples:

NodeCreated

↓

Search

↓

Graph

↓

Timeline

↓

UI Refresh

Avoid direct module coupling.

---

# Phase 6 — Search Engine

Complete Search.

Implement:

- Incremental indexing
- Live indexing
- Ranking
- Filters
- Keyboard navigation
- Recent searches
- Search history

Index:

- Projects
- Nodes
- Cards
- Relationships
- Timeline
- Templates

Search communicates only through Repository events.

---

# Phase 7 — Graph Engine

Complete Graph.

Implement:

- Pan
- Zoom
- Selection
- Multi-selection
- Drag
- Highlighting
- Filtering
- Large-project optimization

Graph updates automatically through Events.

---

# Phase 8 — Import / Export

Complete Import and Export.

Import:

- Validation
- Migration
- Duplicate detection
- Recovery

Export:

- Complete projects
- Partial exports
- Templates
- Metadata

Guarantee backward compatibility.

---

# Phase 9 — Error Handling

Implement recovery for:

- Missing files
- Corrupted files
- Invalid imports
- Interrupted saves
- Serialization failures
- Repository failures

No silent failures.

Never lose user data.

---

# Phase 10 — Logging

Introduce structured logging.

Log:

- Repository actions
- Commands
- Events
- Import/Export
- Validation failures
- Storage failures
- Performance warnings

Support configurable log levels:

- Debug
- Info
- Warning
- Error

---

# Phase 11 — Performance

Benchmark:

- Startup
- Loading
- Saving
- Searching
- Graph rendering
- Autosave

Target datasets:

- 10,000 Nodes
- 50,000 Cards
- 20,000 Relationships
- 20,000 Timeline Events

Prefer incremental updates.

Avoid repeated full scans.

---

# Phase 12 — Automated Testing

Create:

## Unit Tests

- Domain
- Validation
- Commands
- Serializers

## Repository Tests

- CRUD
- Transactions
- Events

## Storage Tests

- Save
- Load
- Recovery
- Corruption

## Integration Tests

Verify:

UI ↔ Repository

Repository ↔ Validation

Repository ↔ Commands

Repository ↔ Events

Repository ↔ Storage

Search ↔ Repository

Graph ↔ Repository

## Performance Tests

Stress-test large projects.

---

# Phase 13 — Regression Testing

Before every commit:

- Build project
- Run all tests
- Load existing projects
- Save projects
- Reopen projects
- Verify import/export
- Verify undo/redo
- Verify search
- Verify graph

No regressions allowed.

---

# Phase 14 — Git Workflow

Develop in small milestones.

One feature branch per subsystem.

Commit only after:

- Build passes
- Tests pass
- Regression tests pass

Suggested commit format:

feat(search): complete incremental indexing

fix(graph): resolve zoom rendering

test(repository): add CRUD coverage

---

# Phase 15 — Release Readiness

Before Version 1.0 verify:

- No critical bugs
- No data loss
- Stable autosave
- Stable import/export
- Full backward compatibility
- Responsive UI
- Acceptable performance
- Passing automated tests

Only then begin UI polish and release packaging.

---

# Session Workflow

At the beginning of every session:

1. Audit current implementation.
2. Identify incomplete backend systems.
3. Select exactly one milestone.
4. Complete it fully.
5. Verify with tests.
6. Commit.
7. Report progress.

Never jump between unrelated milestones.

---

# Session Report

Always provide:

- Features completed
- Files added
- Files modified
- Tests added
- Bugs fixed
- Performance improvements
- Remaining issues
- Next milestone
- Estimated completion percentage

---

# Engineering Principle

Act as a senior backend engineer maintaining a production application.

Optimize for:

- Reliability
- Maintainability
- Scalability
- Stability
- Performance
- Testability

Writing more code is not the objective.

Writing production-quality code is.
:::

It mirrors how experienced backend teams work: **foundation → infrastructure → reliability → testing → release**. Since LoreCanvas is now around **85% architecturally complete**, this is the mindset Claude should adopt for the remainder of development.

:::writing{variant="document" id="50831"}
# LCD-018 — Publishing & Export Pipeline Specification

**Version:** 1.0  
**Project:** LoreCanvas  
**Document Type:** LCD (LoreCanvas Design Document)

---

# 1. Purpose

The Publishing & Export Pipeline is responsible for converting a completed LoreCanvas project into publication-ready formats for external writing platforms, ebook readers, and document editors.

The pipeline should transform a finished story into a professionally formatted manuscript while removing development-only information such as worldbuilding notes, internal references, and planning data.

This system represents the final stage of the author's workflow.

---

# 2. Objectives

The Publishing System shall:

- Compile completed stories.
- Preserve chapter order.
- Preserve formatting.
- Generate publication-ready files.
- Support multiple export formats.
- Support platform-specific formatting presets.
- Maintain compatibility with future publishing platforms.

---

# 3. Publishing Workflow

```text
Project
      ↓
Select Story
      ↓
Compile Chapters
      ↓
Validate Story
      ↓
Apply Export Profile
      ↓
Generate Output
      ↓
Preview
      ↓
Export
```

---

# 4. Story Compilation

Before export the system shall:

- Gather all story chapters.
- Sort chapters automatically.
- Merge chapter content.
- Preserve headings.
- Preserve scene breaks.
- Preserve formatting.
- Generate a table of contents when supported.

---

# 5. Story Validation

Before publishing verify:

- Missing chapters
- Empty chapters
- Duplicate chapter numbers
- Broken chapter order
- Invalid formatting
- Missing title
- Missing author name (optional)
- Missing cover image (optional)

Warnings should never modify the user's work automatically.

---

# 6. Publish Workspace

A dedicated **Publish** section shall exist.

Features include:

- Story selection
- Export format
- Platform preset
- Preview
- Metadata editor
- Export history
- Export settings

---

# 7. Metadata

Supported metadata:

- Title
- Subtitle
- Author
- Pen Name
- Description
- Genre
- Tags
- Language
- Copyright
- Series Name
- Volume Number
- Cover Image

Metadata is stored separately from story content.

---

# 8. Platform Export Presets

## AO3

Generate HTML optimized for AO3.

Support:

- Bold
- Italics
- Underline
- Scene breaks
- Chapter titles
- Author notes
- End notes

Exclude:

- Internal notes
- Worldbuilding data
- Character sheets

---

## Wattpad

Generate DOCX suitable for upload.

Support:

- Chapter export
- Story title
- Cover image reference
- Clean paragraph formatting

Allow:

- Export entire story
- Export selected chapters

---

## Kindle (KDP)

Generate EPUB and DOCX.

Support:

- Embedded Table of Contents
- Front matter
- Copyright page
- Chapter navigation
- Proper heading hierarchy
- Clean typography

Compatible with Kindle Direct Publishing requirements.

---

## PDF

Generate print-ready PDF.

Options:

- A4
- Letter
- Book page size

Support:

- Page numbers
- Headers
- Footers
- Table of contents
- Cover page

---

## EPUB

Generate standards-compliant EPUB.

Support:

- Metadata
- Cover
- Navigation
- Chapter structure

---

## DOCX

Generate editable Microsoft Word documents.

Support:

- Styles
- Headings
- Images
- Page breaks
- Table of contents

---

## Markdown

Generate Markdown suitable for GitHub, Obsidian, and static site generators.

---

## HTML

Generate standalone HTML.

Support:

- CSS styling
- Images
- Navigation
- Table of contents

---

## TXT

Generate plain text.

Strip unsupported formatting.

---

## RTF

Generate Rich Text Format for compatibility with older editors.

---

# 9. Export Profiles

Users may save custom profiles.

Example:

"My Kindle Profile"

Includes:

- EPUB
- Cover image
- Front matter
- Copyright page
- TOC

Profiles are reusable.

---

# 10. Preview

Before exporting display:

- Final formatting
- Chapter order
- Table of contents
- Images
- Metadata

Users may return to editing without losing work.

---

# 11. Export Options

Support:

- Entire story
- Selected chapters
- Story arc
- Volume
- Individual chapter

---

# 12. Image Handling

Support:

- Cover images
- Inline illustrations
- Chapter artwork

Automatically optimize images where appropriate while preserving the originals.

---

# 13. Cleanup Rules

Before export remove:

- Character notes
- Timeline notes
- Plot planning
- Internal comments
- Research notes
- Hidden metadata
- Development-only tags

Only published story content should appear in exported files.

---

# 14. Version Compatibility

Generated files should remain compatible with future versions of LoreCanvas whenever practical.

Older projects should continue exporting correctly after migration.

---

# 15. Export History

Maintain an export history including:

- Date
- Story
- Format
- Profile used
- Success or failure

This allows users to reproduce previous exports.

---

# 16. Error Handling

Handle gracefully:

- Missing cover images
- Invalid metadata
- Unsupported characters
- Failed file generation
- Interrupted export
- Disk write failures

Provide clear messages and preserve user data.

---

# 17. Future Expansion

Design the publishing pipeline so future integrations can be added without redesign.

Potential future targets include:

- Direct publishing APIs
- Blog platforms
- Static website generators
- Additional ebook ecosystems

These should plug into the existing export pipeline rather than replacing it.

---

# 18. Success Criteria

The Publishing & Export Pipeline is complete when it can:

- Compile a finished story.
- Validate publication data.
- Generate platform-ready files.
- Preserve formatting.
- Remove development-only information.
- Produce consistent exports across supported formats.
- Export reliably without data loss.

The Publishing & Export Pipeline represents the final stage of the LoreCanvas workflow, transforming a completed manuscript into a publication-ready work suitable for external platforms and long-term archival.
:::
